# Glider and aeroplane (`glider_aeroplane`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by internal_combustion_engine, laws_of_motion, lever_mechanics_statics
- Core idea: Separate lift from propulsion (Cayley 1799): a fixed, slightly cambered wing meeting the air at a small angle gives lift that grows with wing area and the square of speed, a tailplane and fin keep it stable, and control in three axes (pitch, yaw and roll, by warping the wings or ailerons) lets the pilot balance and turn. A hang glider of willow and cotton, 12–15 m² of wing, carries a man from a hill (Lilienthal, about 2,000 flights). Powered flight needs an engine of about 10 kW weighing under about 100 kg and efficient propellers; human muscle is far too weak for flapping wings.
- Pitfalls:
  - Building Leonardo-style flapping ornithopters powered by muscle
  - Assuming camber or a tail alone guarantees stability; wing incidence, weight distribution and control matter
  - Ignoring roll control; Lilienthal shifted his body weight and was killed in 1896
  - Testing far from the ground before learning control in short low hops
- History: islamic: 9th c. – Abbas ibn Firnas' gliding attempt in Córdoba (reported centuries later); europe: 11th c. – Eilmer of Malmesbury; c. 1485–1505 Leonardo's flight studies; 1799–1853 Cayley; 1891–1896 Lilienthal; americas: 17 Dec 1903 – Wright brothers' powered flights at Kitty Hawk after their own wind-tunnel tests (1901)
- Read:
  - Otto Lilienthal, Der Vogelflug als Grundlage der Fliegekunst (1889)
  - Tom D. Crouch, The Bishop's Boys: A Life of Wilbur and Orville Wright (1989)
  - John D. Anderson Jr., A History of Aerodynamics and Its Impact on Flying Machines (1997)
